title: SPACE AND POLITICAL PARTICIPATION IN POPULAR NEIGHBORHOODS: Insights from the Chilean Urban Uprising
abstract: In this article we examine how space shapes the political dispositions of residents in marginalized neighborhoods and gave form to institutional and contentious participation during the 2019 urban uprising in Chile. Based on qualitative research in two neighborhoods on Santiago's outskirts, we reconstruct residents' engagement with politics prior to and during the urban uprising. We use Lefebvre's relational concept of space in dialogue with Bourdieu's theory of habitus to understand how space (perceived, conceived, lived) interacts with individual resources, mainly cultural capital. This interaction shows that participation strategies during the revolt stemmed from political dispositions developed over time, having been shaped by the diverse and conflicting ways residents perceive, conceive, and live space. These strategies are also influenced by what Bourdieu terms residents' 'volume of capital'. Based on their political dispositions, residents of popular neighborhoods display a varied repertoire of political strategies. These strategies include institutional, collaborative, and oppositional participation, with the aim of resolving their daily material needs, affecting national politics, and challenging the neighborhood's reputation within the city's imagination.

title: Solidarity Economy from the Margins: A Qualitative Study of a Women's Cooperative in Southern Chile from a Feminist Political Economy Perspective
abstract: This article presents a qualitative study drawing on ethnographic methods of Cooperativa de Mujeres Llayin, an Indigenous women-led cooperative in southern Chile. Situated in a Mapuche-Huilliche community, the cooperative illustrates how solidarity economy practices emerge as collective responses to structural exclusions tied to gender, race, and territory. Addressing a gap in the still largely Eurocentric Social and Solidarity Economy (SSE) research, this study integrates Feminist Political Economy (FPE) and the Sustainability of Life Approach (SLA) to explore alternatives to productivist analyses. Fieldwork was conducted between February and April 2024 and included participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and a participatory workshop. Findings show that the cooperative enables a flexible organisation of work adapted to local logics of reciprocity centred on cultural affirmation and collective care, embodying solidarity-based economic practices oriented towards sustaining life rather than bureaucratic or accumulation imperatives. These practices are rooted in the Indigenous community and predate the cooperative's legal constitution. This creates tensions with a public policy that seeks to promote a transition towards greater market integration through formalisation, but shows shortcomings such as limited coordination with the local administrative level, as well as a design inspired by exogenous models that do not necessarily reflect the realities of the territory and the solidarity economy practices that develop within it. From an FPE perspective, the findings further show that, while cooperative work provides flexibility to reconcile productive and reproductive responsibilities, the model itself does not overcome gender biases, and its effects on women's economic autonomy remain limited.

title: From Classroom to Streets: The Effect of Schools on Political Participation Among Chilean Youth
abstract: During the past 20 years, students in Chile have taken center stage in several political demonstrations. In this study, we explore the effects of school-related variables on youth political participation using administrative data on school attendance during protests in October 2019 and survey data from the 2016 International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS). We use the loss of school attendance as a proxy for youth participation in political mobilization. Our results show that openness in classroom discussions at school has a positive association on conventional and non-conventional (legal) political participation. On the other hand, a respectful school environment and parental participation in school activities are associated with a lower attendance loss. Overall, our findings suggest that schools can help prevent illegal forms of political participation, provided that there is a good school environment. Our results highlight the importance of considering the formal and hidden curricula when studying the effect of schools on political participation.

title: Translating the Third World: intellectual mediation and political language in the magazine Arauco (Chile, 1959-1966)
abstract: This article examines the role of the Chilean socialist magazine Arauco (1959-1966) in the reception and appropriation of Third World political experiences during the Cold War. Drawing on intellectual history and the study of political transfers, the article analyzes the magazine's role as a space for mediating ideas, practices, and discourses from Africa, Asia, and non-aligned Europe within the context of debates surrounding Chilean socialism. Its pages addressed diverse experiences, including decolonization processes, non-alignment, and Yugoslav socialism. It is argued that, through the selection and circulation of international material, Arauco fostered a dialogue between these external models and the political-strategic issues and debates of Chilean socialism-such as non-alignment, antiimperialism, worker self-management, and socialist democracy. However, each of these experiences took on distinct meanings, depending on the frames of reference and issues under discussion, giving rise to diverse political, ideological, and symbolic uses.

title: Discursive geographies of extraction: towards a territorialized application of cultural political economy of extractivism in Chile and Peru
abstract: Over the past two decades, amid repeated socio-environmental conflicts, mining in Peru and Chile has been rearticulated as environmentally responsible and indispensable to the global Green Energy Transition. This article examines how the resilience of extractivism is built and renewed under conditions that should instead constrain it. It argues that in Chile and Peru, two of the world's leading copper exporters, economic elites, in alliance with the state, systematically translate moments of crisis into revised discursive strategies, governance adjustments, and territorial interventions that secure accumulation across conjunctures. To trace these mechanisms, the article introduces Discursive Geographies of Extraction (DGE), an approach that bridges Cultural Political Economy and Latin American critical geography. DGE centers territory as the site where abstract imaginaries and governance arrangements acquire material durability, harder to reverse than the discourse or the law that authorized them. Methodologically, it combines critical discourse analysis of mining business associations' reports and media coverage with policy analysis, interviews, and event observation. It examines four conflicts: Conga and Pascua Lama during the commodity boom of 2003-2013, and Las Bambas and Los Bronces Integrado during the post-boom period of 2014-2024. Across these sites, crises function as generative junctures through which developmentalist narratives are reformulated into green and sustainability-oriented economic imaginaries, environmental governance is recalibrated, and productive territories are materially produced. The article shows how socio-territorial conflicts, understood as responses to capitalist contradictions in copper extraction, shape the terms of extractivism's reconfiguration, and how extractive industries adapt and shape contemporary green capitalism in Latin America.

title: Emotional reactions to referendum campaigns: how news consumption and political orientations made Chileans feel about the constitutional process
abstract: To what extent are emotions shaped by news consumption and political orientations during a referendum campaign? This is the question our study addresses based on the 2022 Chilean Constitutional Referendum, a fraught process initiated with wide citizen support which, nonetheless, ended in citizen rejection at the polls. Using data from a two-wave panel survey, we test complementary models using positive and negative emotions as dependent variables. Our findings confirm that emotions about the referendum are contingent upon certain news consumption regimes. Additionally, we found that individuals on the right and those who rejected the proposal (the "winning" option in the referendum) experienced more negative emotions, suggesting the existence of a group of "sore winners". We discuss how these findings expand previous research about the interaction between news consumption, political orientations and emotions in referendum campaigns.

title: 'When you live the problem, it is different': political representation of people with disabilities in Chile
abstract: This article analyzes the campaign experiences of eighteen candidates with disabilities in the 2021 Chilean Constitutional Convention election, facilitated by a mandatory candidate-list quota that operated alongside stronger inclusion mechanisms (gender parity and reserved seats for indigenous peoples) for other underrepresented groups. While the quota ensured inclusion in party lists, it failed to guarantee seats in the Convention, and only one candidate with a disability was elected. Drawing on semi-structured interviews analyzed thematically, the study explores candidates' motivations for running, the barriers they confronted, and the strategies they deployed during the campaign. The central finding is the emergence of 'experiential representation': participants argued that the lived experience of disability grants unique, irreplaceable knowledge necessary for effective representation, particularly under conditions of constitutional refoundation. Although electoral success was limited, candidates' participation carried strong symbolic value, while exposing how quota design unevenly opens political space across the heterogeneous disability community.

title: The Political Cost of Gabriel Boric's Pardons in Chile: A Process-Tracing Analysis
abstract: Objective/context: On December 30, 2022, Chilean President Gabriel Boric granted 13 pardons. The decision drew widespread rejection from both the opposition and the public, causing various disruptive effects for the government, the most significant of which was a ministerial turnover. Why did the pardons generate such effects? This article argues that, under certain conditions, granting pardons increases the political cost for the government. The objective is to explain the causal mechanism that led to this increase. Methodology: This article uses process tracing to identify the causal mechanism linking the granting of pardons (input) to a ministerial turnover (output). Through sequential analysis of events and available empirical evidence, it traces the causal forces that explain how the presidential decision increased the political cost for the government and led to ministerial changes. Conclusions: The results demonstrate that the political cost increased at two points in the process. The first was driven by legislative opposition and the breakdown of negotiations surrounding the Security Roundtable. The second was tied to the conflict with the Judiciary. Originality: Pardon power often overlooked in Latin American political science. Thus, this article is a theoretical contribution that integrates the literature on the pardon power with the concept of political cost to explain the consequences of pardons for government. Methodologically, it uses process tracing to analyze the political effects of pardons in Latin American democracies.

title: STORIES OF RESISTANCE: AN ANALYSIS OF FORCE DYNAMICS IN TESTIMONIES OF POLITICAL IMPRISONMENT IN CHILE
abstract: The objective of this research is to describe the force dynamics that emerge in the testimonies of former political prisoners of the civil-military dictatorship in Chile. This research is grounded in the principles of cognitive linguistics, force dynamics, and testimonial discourse. The methodology is qualitative, based on grounded theory and the constant comparative method. The corpus consists of 30 testimonies from former political prisoners compiled in the book Cien voces rompen el silencio: Testimonios de expresas y presos politicos de la dictadura militar en Chile (1973-1990), edited by Wally Kunstmann and Victoria Torres. The analysis was conducted using the model proposed by Leonard Talmy, which allows the description of force dynamics that are applied in language. The analysis identified patterns in which the majority of the agonists were the people that gave their testimonies, while the antagonists were represented primarily by members of the Armed Forces and the dictatorship.

title: From America to Spain: Internationalism and Political Transfer in the Socialist Party of Chile (1933-1939)
abstract: This article analyses the international experiences that shaped the political culture of the Chilean Socialist Party during its formative decade (1933-1939), focusing on the processes of political transfer and militant reinterpretation. From a transnational perspective, it examines how Latin American and European models were selectively appropriated and rearticulated within the party's ideological and strategic framework. The study is based on a qualitative analysis of the party press, parliamentary debates and militant publications. It argues that the PSCh moved from an anti-imperialist Latin Americanism towards an anti-fascist and democratic internationalism. In an initial phase (1933-1935), the Chaco War and Mexican Cardenism served to develop critiques of imperialism and the agrarian structure. Subsequently (1936-1939), the Spanish Civil War and the Popular Front consolidated anti-fascism as a central organising principle.

title: Memory and Political Culture Across Generations of Chilean Economic Elites
abstract: This article explores how Chilean business elites remember the Unidad Popular (UP) government (1970-1973) and how these memories shape their current political culture. Drawing on interviews, it distinguishes between two generational groups: those who experienced the UP as adults and those who lived through it as children or adolescents or did not live it firsthand. The study examines how memories of political confrontations and commodity shortages form a conservative collective narrative that resists systemic reform. These recollections often legitimize the 1973 military coup and the subsequent neoliberal transformations. The research shows that personal experiences, as well as narratives passed down through generations, contribute to the construction of a political culture among economic elites that privileges stability over change. By analyzing these memory dynamics, the article underscores the importance of elite historical consciousness in shaping their vision of Chile's political present and its possible future.

title: Think Tanks and Political Crises in Chile, 2011-2022; or, The Crystallization of the Intellectual Infrastructure in a Middle-Income Country
abstract: Why did Chile's think tank sector become more concentrated even as supply and demand for expert opinion expanded? This article examines nine organizations between 2011 and 2022, tracking 18,948 public interventions and conducting sixty-six interviews with think tank members and stakeholders to understand this apparent paradox. While political crises, from student movements to the 2019 social "outbreak" offered opportunities for new voices to emerge, established think tanks systematically consolidated their advantages. This article develops the concept of intellectual infrastructure-the material, institutional, technological, and network conditions enabling expert interventions-to explain how advantages in funding and media access become self-reinforcing. In a middle-income country where international funding dried up without the emergence of domestic philanthropy, organizations with larger, more flexibly allocated resources could effectively crowd out competitors. This challenges assumptions about expertise democratization, revealing how intellectual authority becomes concentrated even during periods of apparent openness.& iquest;Por qu & eacute; el ecosistema de think tanks en Chile se volvi & oacute; m & aacute;s concentrado incluso despu & eacute;s de que tanto la oferta como la demanda de opini & oacute;n experta se expandieran? Este art & iacute;culo examina nueve organizaciones entre 2011 y 2022, utilizando 18.948 intervenciones p & uacute;blicas y sesenta y seis entrevistas con miembros de think tanks y otros actores relevantes para comprender esta paradoja. Si bien las crisis pol & iacute;ticas -desde movimientos estudiantiles hasta el "estallido social"- ofrecieron oportunidades para que surgieran nuevas voces, los think tanks establecidos consolidaron sistem & aacute;ticamente sus ventajas. Este art & iacute;culo desarrolla el concepto de infraestructura intelectual -las condiciones materiales, institucionales, tecnol & oacute;gicas y de redes que posibilitan las intervenciones p & uacute;blicas- para explicar c & oacute;mo ventajas en financiamiento y acceso a los medios tienden a perpetuarse. En un pa & iacute;s de ingreso medio donde el financiamiento internacional se agot & oacute; sin que emergiera una filantrop & iacute;a local, las organizaciones con recursos m & aacute;s amplios y asignados con mayor flexibilidad pudieron efectivamente "desplazar" a sus competidores. title: Modulaciones etnotécnicas: patrimonialización, extractivismo minero y economía política del pasado en el salar de Atacama (norte de Chile)
abstract: This article examines how Indigenous Atacame & ntilde;o Communities mobilize the past as a political and economic resource amid lithium extraction in northern Chile. Based on ethnographic research in the Salar de Atacama basin, as well as archival work on regional archaeology, it develops the concept of ethnotechnical modulation to describe how archaeological knowledge, heritage discourses, and narratives of deep historical continuity are articulated with contemporary Indigenous politics and extractive economies. Over the past decades, narratives of millennia-long occupation of the desert-largely produced through archaeological research and museum practices-have become central to Atacame & ntilde;o territorial claims. Community leaders mobilize these historical narratives in negotiations with the Chilean state and lithium companies, particularly in agreements that channel financial transfers to Atacame & ntilde;o communities. These arrangements should not be understood simply as heritage politics or corporate compensation, but as a form of modulation of the past that articulates an Atacame & ntilde;o position at the limits of the state and its extractive political economy, one that is neither fully captured by governance nor adequately described as resistance.Este art & iacute;culo examina c & oacute;mo las Comunidades Atacame & ntilde;as movilizan el pasado como recurso pol & iacute;tico y econ & oacute;mico en el contexto de la extracci & oacute;n de litio en el norte de Chile. A partir de una investigaci & oacute;n etnogr & aacute;fica en la cuenca del salar de Atacama y trabajo de archivo sobre la arqueolog & iacute;a regional, se desarrolla el concepto de modulaci & oacute;n etnot & eacute;cnica para describir la articulaci & oacute;n entre conocimiento arqueol & oacute;gico, discursos patrimoniales, narrativas de continuidad cultural, pol & iacute;tica ind & iacute;gena contempor & aacute;nea y econom & iacute;as extractivas. En este contexto, las narrativas de ocupaci & oacute;n milenaria del desierto de las & uacute;ltimas d & eacute;cadas, producidas en gran medida por la arqueolog & iacute;a y las pr & aacute;cticas museogr & aacute;ficas, se han vuelto centrales para las reivindicaciones territoriales atacame & ntilde;as, pues las comunidades las movilizan en negociaciones con el Estado chileno y con las empresas del litio, especialmente en el marco de acuerdos que canalizan las transferencias financieras. Estos arreglos no deben ser entendidos simplemente como parte de un proceso de patrimonializaci & oacute;n o de compensaci & oacute;n corporativa, sino m & aacute;s bien desde una forma de modulaci & oacute;n del pasado que articula lo atacame & ntilde;o como una posici & oacute;n liminal del Estado y su econom & iacute;a pol & iacute;tica extractivista, la cual no se reduce al binario dominaci & oacute;n/resistencia.

title: ELECTORS AND PARLIAMENTARIANS BETWEEN TWO SHORES: RELATIONS AND POLITICAL REPRESENTATION AMONG THE CHILEAN COMMUNITY RESIDING IN SPAIN, 1810-1820
abstract: Based on an analysis of the electoral documentation of the convocation of the Cortes in 1810 and 1820, and employing a prosopographical approach, this article focuses on the Chilean community residing in Spain during a period of profound institutional uncertainty. In this context, beyond political activity, permeated the daily lives of individuals and conditioned their life trajectories. From the perspective of migration, this study examines the characteristics that defined the electoral body and how these were projected onto political identities and positions that were still in progress, ranging from alignment with the interests of the capital's elite to an increasing disconnection from the groups they represented. The aim is to identify lines of continuity and difference between the profiles of the individuals who exercised political representation of Chile in the Peninsula in both electoral processes. Furthermore, this study aims to open up possibilities for a deeper analysis of the political space during a period defined by the crisis of the hispanic monarchy, the unraveling of colonial relationships, and the configuration of the emerging Latin American state realities.

abstract: | This article explores the intersections between migratory trajectories, processes of political subjectivation, and forms of involvement in migration struggles in Chile. Its aim is to capture the heterogeneous ways in which migrants become politically constituted through these struggles, while also considering the specific imprint that foreignness leaves on this process. It further reflects on how these intersections contribute to reshaping citizenship in Chile as an emerging destination within South-South migration flows. The analysis draws on discourse analysis of a corpus of life histories from 45 migrants engaged in social and political organisations across three regions of Chile (Tarapac & aacute;, Antofagasta, and the Metropolitan Region), through which four main types of intersection are identified. Particular attention is given to trajectories of political subjectivation that originate in involvement in migration struggles in the country of residence, especially those driven by demands for the right to housing and to the city. The article argues that such struggles give rise to territorialised acts of citizenship, where new forms of political and civic subjectivation emerge alongside alternative ways of constructing sociopolitical ties and relating to the state.

title: Political and Mobilization Cycles in Neoliberal Chile: Workers, Pobladores, and Students
abstract: This article addresses the recent Chilean cycle of mobilizations (2006-2019) by focusing on three movements that played leading roles in resistance from the dictatorship to the social uprising: students, unions, and pobladores, showing how they interacted with and contributed to shaping the political-electoral cycle of the past decade. Although the resurgence of social mobilizations in Chile opened the possibility of a constitutional process, the latter's failure goes hand in hand with the questioning of the democratic nature of contentious collective action. Nonetheless, current Chilean society continues to demand change, and social movements remain fundamental for pressuring for change and channeling discontent into political expression. This means that social movements are intrinsic to democracy and its renewal.Este art & iacute;culo analiza el ciclo de movilizaci & oacute;n reciente (2006-2019) en Chile, centr & aacute;ndose en tres movimientos protag & oacute;nicos tanto de la resistencia a la dictadura como del estallido social: el movimiento estudiantil, sindical y de pobladores; mostrando c & oacute;mo dicho ciclo ha interactuado y contribuido a modelar el ciclo pol & iacute;tico-electoral de la & uacute;ltima d & eacute;cada. Aunque el resurgimiento de las movilizaciones sociales en Chile abri & oacute; la posibilidad de un proceso constitucional, su fracaso ha ido de la mano con una desvalorizaci & oacute;n y cuestionamiento de la acci & oacute;n colectiva contenciosa, mostr & aacute;ndola como potencialmente amenazante para la democracia. Pese a ello, la sociedad chilena hoy sigue demandando cambios y los movimientos sociales contin & uacute;an siendo fundamentales para presionar por ellos y canalizar el descontento para que se exprese pol & iacute;ticamente, mostrando que movilizaciones sociales son un elemento consustancial a la democracia, oxigen & aacute;ndola y permitiendo su correcci & oacute;n.

title: Invited but Ignored: The Political Participation of Indigenous People in Chile's Constitutional Process
abstract: Chile is considered an outlier compared to other Latin American countries, where Indigenous demands have had significant effects on state reforms and the broader political landscape. The constitutional process initiated in 2019 opened new avenues for Indigenous political participation. In this article, we analyze the interactions among Indigenous and non-Indigenous collectives during the constitutional process through the lens of indigenismo. Drawing on Situational Analysis, we examine how different social worlds engaged with questions of identity, representation, and political rights throughout the constitutional process. The findings show that Indigenous participation was characterized by tensions between the promises of expanded political participation and the institutional and political forces that constrained their influence. These interactions reveal struggles to represent Indigenous communities within state institutions, where they are invited but often ignored. The article contributes to broader discussions about Indigenous political participation and the evolving role of indigenismo in contemporary Latin American politics.Chile es at & iacute;pico en comparaci & oacute;n con otros pa & iacute;ses latinoamericanos, donde las demandas ind & iacute;genas han tenido efectos significativos en reformas estatales y en el panorama pol & iacute;tico amplio. El proceso constitucional iniciado en 2019 abri & oacute; nuevas v & iacute;as para la participaci & oacute;n ind & iacute;gena. En este art & iacute;culo, analizamos las interacciones entre colectivos ind & iacute;genas y no ind & iacute;genas durante el proceso constitucional a trav & eacute;s del lente del indigenismo. Basados en el An & aacute;lisis Situacional, examinamos c & oacute;mo distintos mundos sociales se involucraron en temas de identidad, representaci & oacute;n y derechos a lo largo del proceso. Argumentamos que la participaci & oacute;n ind & iacute;gena estuvo caracterizada por tensiones entre promesas de mayor participaci & oacute;n pol & iacute;tica y las fuerzas institucionales y pol & iacute;ticas que limitaron su influencia. Estas interacciones revelan disputas de representaci & oacute;n de las comunidades ind & iacute;genas, las que son invitadas a instituciones estatales pero frecuentemente ignoradas. El art & iacute;culo contribuye a los debates sobre participaci & oacute;n pol & iacute;tica ind & iacute;gena y el papel del indigenismo en la pol & iacute;tica latinoamericana contempor & aacute;nea.

title: Learning From the Past to Read the Present: Political Crisis, Democratization, and Double Movement in Early Twentieth-Century Chile
abstract: This article analyses the cycle of social and political conflict that unfolded in Chile in the early twentieth century. It focuses on the uncertainty-rich phase of 1918-1925 as a critical juncture that opened competing institutional pathways. Leaning on democratization studies and on Polanyi's double movement approach, the article conceptualizes capitalist dislocation as a main trigger of the crisis and of the emerging protective demands from that period. This perspective is introduced an analytical framework for examining Chilean specific democratic pathway. Empirically, the study draws on case study method. In that line, and in order to gain deeper understanding of political conflict debates of the period a systematic qualitative analysis of press debates across ideologically diverse outlets (1918-1925), complemented by secondary scholarship extending from the late nineteenth century to the late 1930s.

title: Photography, aesthetics, and resistance in Chile: political imageries under the lens of Armindo Cardoso
abstract: This article defines the notion of political imagery of 70s Chile by examining the Portuguese Armindo Cardoso's photographs made in Chile between 1969 and 1973. Through the lens of civil-contract ethics, immigrant duality, and text - image interplay, the study shows how placards, banners and captions work not as ancillary context but as rhetorical agents that mobilise viewers. A curated corpus of eleven images, selected by provenance, display, and reuse history (urban rallies, Mapuche assemblies and agrarian reform scenes) is analysed in relation to Chile's visual field of the period, highlighting how Cardoso's exilic viewpoint negotiates attachment and distance to stage collective agency while respecting ethical exposure. The article also reconstructs the buried archive's material itinerary (1973-2013), clarifying issues of provenance, access and mediation. By situating these visual practices within broader debates on memory politics and post-documentary aesthetics, the article offers visual studies a transferable analytic for understanding how photographic images create civic publics and politicise their own afterlives.

title: From the Concertación to the Nueva Mayoría: The controlled political shift in Chile's 2013 presidential election
abstract: This article examines Chile's 2013 electoral process as a turning point in the country's recent political trajectory, focusing on the transition from the Concertaci & oacute;n to the Nueva Mayor & iacute;a. Using a historical case-study design and an explanatory approach, it traces the reconfiguration of the system of coalitions and analyzes the selection of presidential candidates, focusing on the first legally binding primaries and the difficulties in nominating a candidate in the governing party. The study draws primarily on official electoral results, complemented by national press archives and academic scholarship on primaries, party systems, and electoral behavior. Findings indicate that the election favored Michelle Bachelet and that, despite unprecedented candidate fragmentation and rising abstention, the outcome was shaped by the persistence of bi-coalitionism. The article concludes that the 2013 turn amounted to a controlled political shift-a strategic expansion of the center-left through the Nueva Mayor & iacute;a that strengthened coordination and electoral advantage without institutional rupture, while foreshadowing more disruptive realignments in subsequent electoral cycles.

title: How to Align Science and Politics in the Context of Competitive Funding: An Analysis of Political Interest in Science and Public Fund Allocation in Chile (1982-2021)
abstract: This article examines the relationship between the principles of scientific excellence and equity in national science policy in Chile, a semi-peripheral country. It seeks to understand how political priorities influence the distribution of scientific resources and how these influences interact with disciplinary and institutional contexts. The study analyzes data on the allocation of publicly funded scientific projects in Chile 1982-2021. This quantitative dataset is complemented by a qualitative review of presidential speeches and institutional policy documents from the same period, enabling a contextual interpretation of the findings. The findings indicate that political priorities are reflected in project allocations, particularly through the promotion of certain research topics and increasing attention to gender and territorial equity. Yet, the influence of political agendas is mediated by contextual variables such as disciplinary area, the trajectories of scientific communities, and the structure of the research ecosystem. The analysis reveals a dynamic of "negotiated autonomy," in which political influence on science is present but shaped by institutional and disciplinary factors. These dynamics highlight the complex interplay between equity, excellence, and governance in the design and implementation of science policy in Chile.(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic) title: From fragmented to integrated sustainability in lithium extraction? Political measurements and critical minerals in times of sociotechnical transition in Chile
abstract: Lithium, a critical mineral for the global energy transition, has positioned Chile as one of the world's leading producers through brine-based extraction. From this case, we identify a broader dynamic that we named "fragmented sustainability", in which researchers and policymakers assess the lithium extraction through isolated environmental, economic, social and cultural dimensions. This fragmentation limits the capacity of sustainability science to address the complexity of critical mineral extraction. We argue for the need to move toward integrated sustainability as both a research and political challenge. Drawing on Science and Technology Studies (STS), we conceptualize measurement practices as political acts that not only describe but also participate in constructing socio-technical realities. From this perspective, advancing sustainability requires rethinking how extraction is measured and governed. We call for integrated measurement frameworks that connect environmental, economic, social and cultural indicators, while also incorporating diverse scientific, local, and ancestral knowledges. Such plural and situated approaches can transform sustainability from a fragmented ideal into a grounded practice, enabling more just and context-sensitive transitions in the governance of critical minerals.

title: Political Subjectification on TikTok: A Postdigital Mode of Inquiry for Tracing Affects Among Chilean Youth
What is Left After the Protest Wave? Tracing Generational Patterns of Political Engagement in the Wake of Chile's Student Movement
abstract: Drawing on Mannheim, we examine how the ebbs and flows of student mobilization have shaped distinct political generations in Chile. We identify four generations forged through key moments of student activism and wider episodes of collective mobilization: the Dictatorship, Democracy, Penguin, and Frontlines generations. We use longitudinal data from the ELSOC study (2016-2023) to trace attitudinal and behavioral patterns of political engagement across cohorts. The findings show that the Penguin and Frontlines generations, socialized during 2006 and 2011-2019 protest cycles, exhibit higher protest levels and electoral participation, especially during the 2019 social uprising and the 2020 plebiscite. They also show stronger digital activism and progressive attitudes, particularly among women. However, generational effects are not static: while early mobilization fosters engagement, demobilization and political fatigue emerge over time, after the 2019 social uprising. Moreover, younger cohorts show declining student movement identification, suggesting a shift in political referents. Our findings indicate that protest waves can shape enduring political dispositions, but these may change as individuals and their political contexts evolve. Generational identities are thus dynamic, contingent on formative experiences and subsequent developments. Understanding these dynamics is crucial, as the endurance of political generations can shape the long-term durability of student movement outcomes.

title: Applying the rural territorial development approach in designing a regional policy in Atacama, Chile Aplicacao da abordagem do desenvolvimento territorial rural para desenhar uma politica regional no Atacama, Chile
abstract: Rural territorial development emerged as an evolution of regional economics and local development, emphasizing strategies adapted to the specific characteristics of each territory. Chile's National Rural Development Policy, enacted in 2020, aligned with this perspective. In 2021, three pilot projects were implemented to develop regional versions of the National Rural Development Policy, including one in the Atacama Region, which is the case study of this research. The purpose was to examine the dynamics and outcomes of translating a national policy framework, based on the contextual approach of the rural territorial development, to a specific territorial scale. The methodology comprised the collection of field information to conduct a gap analysis and the formulation of a regional public policy proposal. The findings underscored the benefits of the rural territorial development approach in understanding the complexity of rural territories, while revealing challenges to its effective application.

title: Psychometric study of the political violence support scale in a sample of Chilean university students
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the psychometric properties of reliability and validity of the Political Violence Support (PVS) scale in a sample of Chilean university students. A cross-sectional design and non-probabilistic convenience sampling were employed, involving 480 participants (61% women, 37.8% men, and 1.2% other gender), aged between 18 and 45 years (M = 21.35; SD = 2.93). The results obtained through structural equation modelling confirmed the unidimensionality of the PVS, with adequate fit indicators and satisfactory levels of reliability, as indicated by internal consistency. Criterion validity showed positive and significant correlations of small effect size with all dimensions of the Left-Wing Authoritarianism (LWA) scale and with one dimension of the Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA) scale. Furthermore, factor invariance analyses provided evidence of configural, metric, and scalar equivalence across sex and age groups. Collectively, the results support the use of the adapted version of the PVS for assessing attitudes that support political violence among Chilean university students.

title: Citizens' perceptions of the Chilean social outburst: environmental collective action willingness and the role of political identification, democracy, and gender
abstract: This study examines citizens' perceptions of the 2019 Chilean social outburst using cross-sectional survey data from a stratified probabilistic sample of 809 adults in the Valpara & iacute;so Region, Chile. We analyse how environmental collective action willingness, political identification, attitudes toward democracy, and gender are associated with evaluations of the protest movement. Descriptive analyses and a General Linear Model (ANCOVA) were estimated, controlling for age, educational level, and participation in social organisations; multiple linear regression models were additionally used as robustness checks. The results indicate that environmental collective action willingness constitute the strongest and most robust correlate of positive evaluations of the social outburst, followed by political identification, with respondents identifying with the left reporting more favourable perceptions than those identifying with the right. In contrast, attitudes toward democracy and gender do not exhibit independent effects in the fully adjusted model, while age introduces a consistent generational gradient. Overall, the findings suggest that perceptions of the Chilean social outburst are structured primarily by dispositional orientations toward collective action and, to a lesser extent, by ideological positioning, rather than by normative evaluations of democracy.

title: Informal settlements in Valparaíso (Chile): mobilized knowledge of communities and political position of municipalities
abstract: The housing deficit in Chile has led to an explosive growth of informal settlements. Although investment in housing subsidies has been a priority in public policy, informal settlements continue to grow, reflecting a multidimensional and dynamic problem. Using a qualitative approach that combines focus groups and interviews with residents of settlements in the Metropolitan Area of Valpara & iacute;so and municipal officials, the study analyzes the knowledge and strategies mobilized by communities, as well as the municipalities' perspectives on this process. Organized actions are observed for land subdivision, street layout, housing construction, infrastructure network connections, and public spaces. Additionally, mechanisms for conflict resolution and negotiation strategies with public and private actors are discussed. These knowledge and practices in the construction and management of habitat enable valuable community-public institutional articulations, which are key to advancing a new policy for settlement and community management. This self-management of habitat challenges the State's structure in ways that demonstrate participatory, mobilizing, and democratic management. Urban informality is not a homogeneous process but different assemblages between institutions and communities generating agreements, processes, and differentiated and dynamic spaces.

title: Between Hatred and Silence: the Psychosocial Impact of Heterocisnormative-Masculinizing Discourses and Practices in Political Discourse Toward LGBTIQA plus People in the 2025 Chilean Presidential Election
abstract: IntroductionThis article analyzes how LGBTIQA+ people living in two urban contexts in Chile (Santiago and Talca) experience the combination of openly hostile discourses from far-right candidacies and the strategic silences of sectors that define themselves as progressive in the context of the 2025 presidential election.MethodsDrawing on a qualitative study based on interviews and focus groups with eight LGBTIQA+ participants, a reflexive thematic analysis was conducted to identify patterns of shared meaning.ResultsThree thematic axes are presented: (a) anticipatory fear in the face of the advance of conservative and ultraconservative sectors, experienced as a concrete threat to the continuity of rights and to physical integrity; (b) selective safety and the experience of second-class citizenship, in which state protection is perceived as a privilege restricted to normative bodies; and (c) complicit silences on the part of progressive blocs, the instrumental use of sexual and gender dissidence, and the subjective effects on life projects, decisions regarding legal gender transition, and fantasies of political asylum.ConclusionsThe findings show how political debate in Chile, by reproducing heterocisnormative discourses and practices, both explicit and through silence, creates spaces of distress for LGBTIQA+ populations. Policy Implications: Implications for public policy, professional practice, and future research are discussed, particularly the need to address heterocisnormative and masculinizing discourses and practices in political narratives as constitutive of structural violence and thereby mitigate their negative effects on LGBTIQA+ people.

title: Privatizing Social Rights: The Law and Political Economy of Chile's Pension Transformation
abstract: Chile's pension privatization represents one of the most radical neoliberal experiments in social security reform, reshaping welfare from a collective right into a market-driven, property-based entitlement. This Article examines how the constitutionalization of pension privatization entrenched inequalities, shielding the system from democratic contestation and embedding a logic of over-propertization, where private property rights supersede social rights. Drawing on a Law and Political Economy (LPE) approach, explicitly concerned with the distributional consequences of legal design, this study traces how, during the Pinochet dictatorship (1973-90), Chile's 1980 Constitution, and Decree Law 3500 institutionalized financialization and individual responsibility, transforming social security into an asset class managed by private pension fund administrators (AFPs). By legally structuring private capitalization accounts as financial assets with attributes such as ownership, transferability, and enforceability, these frameworks granted private actors control over investment management and risk distribution. The analysis highlights challenges to reversing this model, as judicial claims, pension fund withdrawals during COVID-19, and two failed constitution-making processes reveal legal and political constraints on reform. It examines legislative efforts, judicial interpretations, and collective mobilizations-such as the No+AFP campaign-seeking to restore solidarity. It also explores legitimation strategies, including the discourse of "popular capitalism" and the institutional entrenchment of AFPs within Chile's political economy. By framing pension privatization as a constitutional and legal project rather than mere economic policy, this Article underscores the global consequences of over-propertization and the urgency of reimagining social rights. In doing so, it contributes to a growing body of LPE scholarship that treats constitutions as terrains of economic power, exposing how legal frameworks both encode and contest neoliberal orders.

title: SOCIO-POLITICAL NARRATIVES ABOUT THE CHILE OF THE PRESENT: TRANSITION TO DEMOCRACY AND SOCIAL EXPLOSION: A PRELIMINARY ASSESSMENT
abstract: The Chile of the present has been marked, by the intellectual political debate regarding whether the Chilean transition is over or whether its end is still pending, even more so, with the two constituent processes that have been promoted in recent years. However, beyond that, much of the existing literature continues to debate an extensive and unfinished Chilean transition, to which is added the controversy regarding the origins, causes and characteristics of the social outbreak of 2019. Based on the above, the following article has the general objective of identifying, characterizing and accounting for those socio-political narratives.

abstract: Over the past decade, Chile has experienced a sustained decline in birth rates, along with a progressive increase in maternal age at the time of first pregnancy. This phenomenon reflects demographic and sociocultural dynamics with significant implications for health planning and public policy. Methods: An ecological study was conducted using aggregated data from the National Institute of Statistics (INE) for the period 2010-2022. Trends in overall birth rates and age-specific fertility rates were described, as well as changes in the relative contribution of each maternal age group to the total number of births. Results: The number of births in Chile declined by 24.5% between 2010 and 2022. Fertility among women aged 15 to 24 showed a marked decrease, while the proportion of births among women aged 30 and over increased steadily. A progressive shift in the reproductive timeline toward older maternal age groups was observed. Discussion: Chile is undergoing an advanced stage of demographic transition, characterized by delayed motherhood. This shift is associated with higher levels of female education, unequal labor conditions, and structural barriers to balancing work and caregiving. Public policies must adapt to this new scenario through a life-course approach that promotes equity and shared responsibility, strengthening both the prevention of adolescent and for later motherhood.

title: The Personal is Political: Life Course Transitions, Civic Engagement and Participation of Older Women in Chile
abstract: Research on the civic engagement of older women has increased, but specific approaches to political participation and life trajectories from a life course perspective remain scarce. This study explores how life transitions influence and relate to the political participation of older women throughout their lives. We conducted individual interviews with 18 women over the age of 60 who are members of social organisations in Chile. Through thematic analysis, we identified four types of life transitions: those related to family, work, illness, and the socio-political context. These transitions impact participation trajectories, facilitating or hindering participation or permeating the content of civic activities. We discuss the importance of broadening the notion of political participation, highlighting forms of involvement that emerge from everyday experiences linked to caregiving and traditional gender roles, which are often invisible.

title: Punishing the gaze: the eye as a political image of the 2019 Chilean uprising
abstract: This article examines the visual representations of the eye that emerged during the Chilean social uprising of 2019, in direct relation to the systematic ocular injuries caused by police repression. Drawing on a semi-discursive approach, the study analyzes a heterogeneous corpus of urban interventions, artistic productions, and embodied performative practices as visual dispositifs that articulated political meanings in the public sphere. The article integrates perspectives from political theory and visual studies to conceptualize the eye as an iconic act, an expressive formula (pathosformel), and a floating signifier through which violence, visibility, and resistance were negotiated. It argues that these images functioned simultaneously as acts of denunciation-exposing the punitive rationality of state violence- and as forms of symbolic resistance that reconfigured the distribution of the sensible. Rather than merely documenting repression, ocular imagery actively contributed to the production of collective affects, memories, and processes of political subjectivation. By situating these visual practices within broader debates on punishment, agonism, and aesthetic politics, the article contributes to international discussions on visual culture, protest movements, and state violence, offering a critical perspective on the role of images in contemporary social uprisings.

title: The political economy of Chile's coal transition
abstract: In debates about just transitions the experience of unjust coal transitions loom large. Case studies often focus on the experience of countries in Europe and North America, comparing and contrasting more laissez-faire and interventionist state strategies aimed at supporting workers in the transition. In this article, we explore the neglected case of Chile: a country that has retired early most of its coal plants as part of national decarbonisation plan and a Climate Change Framework law which aims to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. We use the case study, based on extensive interviews with government, business and civil society actors, to understand the political economy of just transition in Chile. Described by many as a neo-liberal energy transition, we argue it embodies many of the contradictions of such transitions around the understated role of the state, the invisibilisation and socialisation of the social and ecological costs of transition and shallow forms of democratisation through performative patterns of public participation which seek to manage dissent. We suggest the transition reflects the prevailing model of capitalist extractivism in Chile and a series of settlements between the Chilean state, national and foreign capital contested by social resistance to sacrifice zones, helping to inform debates about neo-liberal energy transitions in general and just transitions in particular.

title: The Selection of Corruption as the Most Important Problem: Scandals, Political Identification, and Public Opinion in Chile (2010-2023)
abstract: This article examines the conditions under which corruption is selected as the most important problem in Chile (2010-2023). From an agenda-setting perspective, it is argued that scandals increase the salience of the issue, while its prioritization depends on political identification. Using data from the CEP survey and fitting logit models, the results show that the occurrence of scandals is associated with the selection of corruption as the most important problem, especially among individuals who identify with the political center. The study highlights the interaction between contextual shocks and political identification in the prioritization of issues.

title: Political convergence and ideology: the case of China-Chile free trade agreement
abstract: PurposeExisting literature on China in the Americas emphasizes trade and economic complementarity, often portraying free trade agreements (FTAs) as technocratic decisions. This paper challenges that view, arguing that such explanations overlook political and ideological dimensions in cases such as the Chile-China FTA - China's first bilateral agreement of this sort signed ever.Design/methodology/approachDrawing on declassified documents (1989-2005) and post-structuralist discourse theory (Essex School), the article conceptualizes international practice as the discursive articulation of foreign policies, using intertextual analysis to identify key signifiers and examine the political divergences, convergences and shared ideological understandings underlying the construction of the FTA.FindingsThe analysis shows that China's WTO aspirations and Chile's open regionalism fostered political convergence around China's market economy status and joint efforts to curb protectionism in the Doha Round. Linking free trade to these convergences reflected a shared ideological understanding that concealed deeper divergences, especially on human rights and Taiwan.Originality/valueThese findings suggest that prospects for China-Americas dialogue depend on complex, context-specific political frameworks (international practices) and challenge conventional narratives that depict relations as depoliticized, driven solely by economic complementarities, or framed around China as a rising power encroaching on the US. backyard.

title: 'Pentecostal spirit and Chilean Pentecostalism' the shift of elective affinities from the political left to the right
abstract: The objective of this article is to analyze two models of being Pentecostal, that is: Pentecostalism and Pentecostalism. These models are in constant dilemma, in a permanent ideological struggle that has led to countless schisms, on the one hand, and to the concentration of power and resources on the part of the pastors. We approach it theoretically from Arnold Toynbee's 'theory of cycles' in complement with the Weberian position of elective affinities. Methodologically we chose four sources: a) Chile Pentecostal magazine, which since 1975 changed its name to La Voz Pentecostal); b) Unpublished documents and minutes of meetings and conferences of pastors; c) news from secular newspapers that published news or reports related to the topic; d) and finally we turn to the academic bibliography that gives an account of the processes that Pentecostalism is experiencing, documented externally since 1940, both from theology and in national literature. As results, we highlight that both religious models are cultural, social, and especially political productions. Being Pentecostal is also being political and being a pastor is being partisan-political.

title: EPISTEMIC PRIVILEGES AND ETHICAL-POLITICAL CHALLENGES: POSSIBLE DIALOGUES ABOUT AFRO-DESCENDANT STUDIES BETWEEN CHILE AND BRAZIL
abstract: In recent years, a broad field of knowledge about Afro-descendant histories, cultures, and political movements has developed in and from Chile. This intellectual production, which has contributed decisively to countering the historical invisibilization of the Afrodescendant population in Chile, has been mobilized in different formats, with different methodological approaches and disciplinary positions, and has unfolded in various forums and publications. Although this research field has developed in dialogue with research and debates in other countries, both in the region and farther away, and has already been subject to important systematization efforts, due to its incipient consolidation there have been few attempts to reflect systematically on the ethical-political and epistemological implications of research about Afro-descendant topics and with Afro-descendant subjects, as well as on the positionality of local research perspectives. In this context, this article takes as a point of departure the challenge presented by an Afro-descendant activist to the researchers who participated in a virtual Afro-descendant studies seminar in 2020. Starting from questions about possible problems of appropriation, extractivism, or epistemic violence, the article advocates for dialogue with frameworks such as afroepistemology or situated knowledge, calling into question the epistemic inequalities and privileges that usually characterize academic knowledge. As a counterpoint, we review the Brazilian debate about racial quotas and the inclusion of quilombola knowledge in universities, tracking their epistemic impact and identifying possible lessons for the Chilean context.

title: The law and political economy of highly detailed constitutional regulations: Lessons from Chile
abstract: This article analyzes the political economy of highly detailed constitutions, using Chile's 2023 constitutional process as a case study. Contrary to traditional constitutional theory favoring broad principles that enable future majorities to shape policy, Chile's second constitutional process approach was markedly different. We argue drafters employed specificity to shield contentious neoliberal economic arrangements from ordinary political debate. By limiting legislative discretion and expanding judicial authority, these provisions ensured fundamental economic policies would be enforced by courts, not decided democratically. This fusion of detailed rules and judicial power represents a distinct constitutional model aimed at circumscribing democratic agency. Within broader Law and Political Economy debates, we contend that such specificity acts less as a guarantor of stability and more as a mechanism of political exclusion, with profound implications for democratic legitimacy.

title: Non-Neutrality of Pedagogy in Early Childhood Education: Ethical, Political, and Epistemological Perspectives of Chilean Female Students
abstract: Initial Teacher Training (ITT) in Early Childhood Education is a key aspect of the education system, requiring high-quality specialization focused on the holistic development of early childhood. In this context, promoting a critical understanding of pedagogy and recognizing its non-neutral nature is crucial in the training of future early childhood educators, acknowledging its ethical, political, and epistemological dimensions. However, the profession suffers from a high level of social devaluation, hindering the recognition of its pedagogical character. From this perspective, the objective of this study was to analyze how students pursuing an online degree in Early Childhood Education at a Chilean university interpret and elaborate on the concept of the non-neutrality of pedagogy, considering its ethical, political, and epistemological dimensions, after a reflective training experience. This study employs a qualitative approach with a descriptive-interpretive design. The unit of analysis consisted of 58 students enrolled in an online Early Childhood Education program at a Chilean university. Data were collected through an online questionnaire with open-ended questions, administered after the students participated in an academic forum reflecting on the ethical, political, and epistemological dimensions of pedagogy. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis with axial coding. The findings of this study show that epistemological, ethical, and political dimensions constitute the main reference points from which the students perceive and interpret that pedagogy cannot be neutral, since it is mediated by values, beliefs, and ideological positions that impact pedagogical decisions. The study concludes that recognizing the non-neutrality of pedagogy, acknowledging that teachers' decisions are mediated by values, beliefs, and positions that guide educational practice, is crucial. title: The USSR and Chile: Political and Economic Challenges during the Popular Unity Government
abstract: This work seeks to answer the question: In what way and what was the political support and the intensity of the economic and financial aid of the Soviet Union to the Chilean government of Salvador Allende? To do this, it takes into account the secondary literature that has been produced in this regard, but, in particular, it includes the consultation that we have been able to make to numerous published documents and that until now were unpublished from official sources of the USSR and the Soviet Communist Party itself. Our hypothesis is that the collaboration provided by Moscow, beyond its promises, was generally limited and of little relevance and was never able to respond to the most pressing needs and emergencies that the Allende government went through, committed to a reform program radicals with socialist connotations.From the study, it seems obvious not so much the reluctance and disbelief of the USSR in the success of the "Chilean path to socialism" as the inability of both sides to build a rational system of economic exchange and assistance of the Chilean government due to internal contradictions and the lack of a clear line of development of its own economy, and bureaucracy, inefficiency, and empty talk of the Soviet side, which was not ready for close cooperation with Chile.

title: Political and health agendas of the presidents of Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay in the context of COVID-19 (2020-2022)
abstract: This paper analyses the political agenda on Twitter of the presidents of Argentina (Alberto Fern & aacute;ndez), Chile (Sebastin Pinera and Gabriel Boric) and Uruguay (Luis Lacalle Pou) during the information management of the health crisis caused by the outbreak of COVID-19. The corpus consists of a sample of 500 messages per actor (2.000 in total), published between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2022, selected using probabilistic and convenience sampling criteria. Using quantitative content analysis, it was determined that the information management of the pandemic was mainly dissemination, with a predominance of the actor themselves and the presidential figure, and with a significant shortage of supporting scientific sources, possibly attributable to the platform's character limitations. Finally, low levels of polarization, negativity and activism were identified. Unlike electoral contexts or explicitly political situations, the context of COVID-19 favored a more informative treatment of relevant issues, aimed at mitigating the damage caused by the virus in the short term.

title: Visual component, ideology and emotions in fact-checked disinformation during Chile's 2022 constitutional process
abstract: This article examines the relationship between disinformation format -items with or without a visual component- and two core content features: ideological bias and affective load. Based on a systematic content analysis of 756 items verified during 2022 by the five main Chilean fact-checking platforms active during the constitutional process, three hypotheses are tested, derived from an integrative model linking dual information processing, affective response and the mobilization of political identification (Brader, 2006; Graber, 1990; Powell et al., 2015). Results show that, contrary to expectations, items with a visual component do not exhibit more ideological bias than purely textual ones, but they do display manifest affective load in a significantly higher proportion. Ideological bias, in both formats, favors right-leaning positions. Exploratory analysis of affective valence reveals an unexpected pattern: positive appeals more than double negative ones (72.6% vs 27.4% within the emotional subset), challenging the dominant view in disinformation research.

title: The Political Ecology of Water Governance and Migration in Chile
abstract: Rural communities in north-central Chile have faced decades-long conflicts over water resources. Although local socio-environmental dynamics have received considerable attention, the related mobility patterns remain underexplored. This study examines the relationship between drought conditions, water governance arrangements, and internal migration flows to and from the province of Petorca. A mixed-methods approach is employed, integrating longterm precipitation anomalies based on Standardised Precipitation Indices (1983-2019), census-based net migration data (1982-2017), and eight semi-structured interviews with local activists, policymakers, and water management experts. Quantitative findings indicate that intensified drought does not lead to increased out-migration; rather, a negative correlation exists between drought and net migration in the province. Interview data highlight the roles of systemic constraints and place attachment in shaping (im)mobility among rural communities, as well as the influx of external actors associated with agribusiness expansion. The study demonstrates how socio-environmental changes, power inequalities, and resource governance influence mobility outcomes in water-stressed regions.

title: Punishment, forgiveness, and forgetting:a history of political imprisonment in Chile
abstract: This article examines the historical evolution of political imprisonment in Chile, analyzing its development and the particularities that have defined its practice in various contexts. Through a historical periodization, political prisoners are identified and characterized, as well as the regulations and conditions that have governed their treatment within the Chilean prison system. The study highlights how political imprisonment reflects dynamics of power, repression, and social inequality, including class struggles and their impact on subsequent generations. With a historiographical approach, this research seeks to contribute to the understanding of political imprisonment as a key category for comprehending Chilean history and its legacies.

title: Operational experience, multi-scalar influence, and political ambivalence: Mechanisms of influence of UNESCO's Regional Bureau for Education in the Chilean school system (1990-2024)
abstract: The UNESCO Regional Bureau for Education in Latin America and the Caribbean (UNESCO/OREALC) is an understudied actor in policy transfer analyses. This article addresses this gap by analyzing the mechanisms of influence and educational messages that the organization mobilizes to shape school policy in Chile, its host country. Drawing on the analysis, processing, and coding of documents produced by the organization between 1990 and 2024, this article demonstrates that UNESCO/OREALC has mobilized and combined diverse, multi-scalar and thematically polyphonic governance instruments within the Chilean education system. The article also shows that UNESCO/OREALC has maintained an ambivalent relationship with Chile, insofar as its mechanisms project narratives of both validation and opposition to local trends of privatization. The article suggests that UNESCO's regional bureau performs functions that transcend the logic of a forum, positioning itself as an actor seeking to broaden the learning curve and policy options within the host country. Furthermore, it reaffirms the identity tensions that arise when the organization operates in contexts with high levels of privatization.

title: Decades of democracy: insights into the political landscape of Chile
abstract: Chile was long considered a beacon of stability in a turbulent region, until the 2019 social outburst and two failed constitutional processes prompted a reassessment. We argue that the reliance of much of the literature on national aggregates obscured underlying dynamics that could have raised institutional alerts, and perhaps even diverted the course of the crisis. To test this claim, we focus on the Chilean party system as it has been tied to the fateful events and ask whether inferences would have been different had alternative data been considered. In this effort, we introduce the Chilean Political Landscape Dataset (CPLD), a standardized longitudinal dataset of district-level electoral outcomes and indicators from 1989 to 2024 that includes more than 5300 observations across legislative, regional, and municipal contests. The dataset allows us to highlight meaningful gaps between prevailing explanations and observed patterns, showing why district-level evidence is necessary to identify the sequence, scope, and ideological contours of change. We show that more detailed data suggest that fragmentation began well before 2015, that the party system was drifting leftward over time, and that fragmentation occurred asymmetrically, impacting parties on the left more than those on the right. We argue that this had previously gone untested and unfound because of the lack of data and conclude by illustrating its relevance by showing additional applications of the CPLD, including assessments of social structures and institutional design.

title: Governance Structures, Political Change and Executive Turnover in State-Owned Enterprises: Evidence From Chile
abstract: To address the shortcomings associated with state ownership, countries have implemented various legal strategies to curb political influence in state-owned enterprises. This research studies whether these strategies constrain the government's ability to use their appointment powers for political considerations. Using logit models, I analyze whether the probability of chief executive officer (CEO) turnover increases once a new government comes into power and whether some state-owned enterprise governance structures (board of directors' independence, ownership models and legal status) can moderate the CEO turnover sensitivity to political change. This study is based on an original dataset of state-owned enterprises' governance characteristics and turnover events in Chile from 2006 to 2023. I find that, while CEOs are more likely to be replaced following a change in government, the turnover sensitivity to political change is heterogeneous among companies with different governance structures. These findings provide insights into what governance mechanisms are the most effective in preventing political interference.

abstract: La implementación de la normativa nacional vigente en Chile, específicamente el Decreto 83 promueve la inclusión educativa en los contextos escolares del país y está dirigida a todas las asignaturas del currículo nacional. Sin embargo, su aplicación práctica en las clases de Educación Física ha sido escasamente estudiada. Esta investigación de tipo cualitativa tuvo por objetivo explorar las percepciones de 12 profesores de Educación Física acerca de la implementación práctica de las directrices nacionales que fomentan la inclusión educativa en los contextos escolares del país. A través de la aplicación de entrevistas semiestructuradas en 3 colegios de Chile, se analizaron las principales apreciaciones y experiencias acerca de fortalezas, debilidades y oportunidades que presenta en la práctica la implementación de la normativa vigente. Los hallazgos revelan que el profesorado de Educación Física conoce las directrices curriculares y la posibilidad de flexibilización de estrategias didácticas, pero existen desafíos sistémicos significativos. Entre ellos, las actitudes hacia estudiantes diversos y la urgencia por fortalecer la formación inicial docente y la formación continua específica en Educación Física para la inclusión, son elementos que tensionan en gran medida la aplicación práctica de la norma. Finalmente, la implementación de la normativa nacional resulta un proceso multifactorial que demanda apoyos contextualizados y cambios culturales propios de la asignatura para el logro de la inclusión educativa genuina.

title: Territorial resistance: A political-emotional dimension in hydroelectric projects in Colombia and Chile
abstract: The purpose of this article is to provide an understanding of territorial resistance from the perspective of social work, as an emotional political dimension. The research considers the experience of people affected by the planning or implementation of hydroelectric projects in Colombia and Chile, through experiential narrative inquiry. The consequences of hydroelectric projects have emerged in Latin America since the 1990s as a new social issue for the discipline, due to the deterioration of inequalities generated by the neoliberal development model. From the analysis of the two cases, it is possible to indicate that resistance in Latin America to hydropower projects has characteristics such as resistance is an ancestral heritage of organizational vision, is a collective action in defense of the permanence of peoples in their territories, and mobilizes efforts in defense of victims of development who demand global solidarity.Territorial resistance: a political-emotional dimension in hydroelectric projects in Colombia and Chile explores the political dimension of emotions in resistance and struggles for territory. Specifically, in communities affected by large-scale hydroelectric projects in Colombia and Chile. This comprehensive analysis delves into how local communities and actors confront the tension between environmental exploitation and their deep connection to the land. Through stories of resistance, the text uncovers the emotional and political challenges that drive communities to defend their territories, highlighting the implications and commitments for Social Work.

title: Bargaining the dark side? Fragmented extractivist governance under hybrid political arrangements in the Chilean copper and lithium industries
abstract: This article examines how bargaining power is exercised by an extractivist state across political arrangements and spatial scales within global extractive production networks. Focusing on Chile's copper and lithium sectors, it introduces the concept of fragmented extractivist governance: a mode through which the state selectively deploys neoliberal, rentier, and developmentalist logics to shape who benefits from, and who bears the costs of, resource-based exploitation. The article contributes empirically by analysing Chile's hybrid governance dynamics, and conceptually by theorizing multiscalar state strategies that (re)produce territorial inequalities, challenging conventional views of state cohesion in extractive economies.

title: Carnival and Revolt: The Political Ambivalence of the 2019 Chilean Estallido
abstract: In this article, I will argue that the perspective of ritual and festive violence related to events such as carnivals, masquerades, or fiestas, needs to be considered alongside economic, structural, and demographic explanations to understand better the phenomenon of social revolts and riots in general, and the Chilean estallido social (social outburst) of 2019 in particular. I propose that only by doing so can we explain the ambiguity of these situations and their varied, often surprising, and complex political outcomes.

title: From political imprisonment to exile: Humanitarian release and/or punishment in the Chilean political transition
abstract: This article contextualizes the historical process that justified the application of the banishment penalty during the Chilean political transition. The commutation of prison sentences to exile was a means of ending the political imprisonment of the Chilean military dictatorship in a context of political and legal debates during the early transition. This measure was part of a mechanism that included policies, special laws, and a discursive framework that transcended the legal nature of the situation, appealing to the fragility of the transition and the need for social peace.

title: Surviving a political regime change: the Communist Party and its members on the critical events of September-December 1973 in Chile
abstract: This article examines the political crisis following the military coup of September 1973, focusing on the four-month period of regime change. The case of Communist Party shows how defeated actors can influence the configuration of authoritarian orders. Forced into clandestinity, the party transformed fear into discipline and survival into political action, compelling the new regime to adjust its repressive mechanisms. By highlighting the role of fear, party discipline, and organizational adaptation, the article contributes to the comparative study of political parties under authoritarianism and their capacity to shape institutional orders.

abstract: Luego del fin de la dictadura cívico-militar en Chile, los gobiernos de la Concertación iniciaron una serie de cambios en el ámbito educativo, incorporando la inclusión educativa como parte de la política educativa. El presente trabajo propone una revisión narrativa de artículos que desarrollan elementos de las políticas de formación inicial docente de los últimos 30 años desde la perspectiva de la inclusión y la justicia social. El artículo analiza los principales lineamientos para la formación docente a partir de las políticas establecidas. Además, propone una serie de interrogantes centradas en cuestionar el rol actual de las facultades de educación para la formación inicial docente desde una perspectiva de justicia social.

title: Co-Management at Peweñentu? A Micro-Political Ecology Perspective of Mapuche Sense of Environmental Justice at Villarrica National Park, Chile
abstract: We examined the sense of justice embraced by Mapuche leaders and activists involved in the conservation and governance of Villarrica National Park. Through this process, we identified three key positions on co-management that reflect two distinct territorial representations of the park. One group emphasized participation and distribution, assigning less importance to recognition as an aspect of justice. In contrast, the other two groups regarded recognition as equally important alongside participation and distribution. According to most Mapuche leaders, communities do not perceive benefits from the park, and some highlighted the negative consequences of establishing this protected area. We conclude by exploring key factors that may influence a potential co-management scenario at the park.
